los.text: Describe that alcohol, obesity and viral hepatitis C are major causes of chronic liver disease in UK
sessions: Case presentation:ALD, Hepatitis C with decompensation
los.html:
• Liver disease is one of the leading causes of premature death in the UK (a major cause of death at 35–49), and deaths have risen sharply over decades, unlike most other major diseases.
CauseUK picture
Alcohol-related liver diseaseThe biggest cause of liver deaths; linked to cheap, widely available alcohol
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly NAFLD)Affects about 1 in 3 adults; driven by obesity and type 2 diabetes; commonest cause of abnormal LFTs
Hepatitis CMainly people who inject drugs (or did); often undiagnosed for years; now curable with direct-acting antivirals
OthersHepatitis B (mostly people from endemic countries), autoimmune hepatitis, PBC, PSC, haemochromatosis, Wilson's, α1-antitrypsin deficiency
  • Common pathway: injury → steatosis → inflammation (steatohepatitis/hepatitis) → fibrosis → cirrhosis → decompensation and hepatocellular carcinoma.

los.text: Explain the patient’s lifestyle as an aetiological factor in chronic liver disease
sessions: Case presentation:ALD, Hepatitis C with decompensation
los.html:
Lifestyle factorLiver effect
Alcohol: amount, pattern (bingeing, daily drinking), dependenceSteatosis, alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis; UK guidance: ≤14 units/week, spread over 3+ days, with drink-free days
Diet, inactivity, obesity, type 2 diabetesMASLD → MASH → cirrhosis
Injecting drug use, sharing equipment, unregulated tattoos, unprotected sex, being born in a high-prevalence countryHepatitis B and C
SmokingFaster fibrosis, HCC
CoffeeProbably protective
Why it matters
  • These causes are modifiable: stopping alcohol
  • Losing 7–10% of body weight
  • and treating hepatitis C can halt or reverse liver damage before cirrhosis
  • So diagnosis is a chance for behaviour change (brief intervention, motivational interviewing).
Combined riskAlcohol and obesity together (and hepatitis C with alcohol) speed up fibrosis more than either alone.

los.text: Recognise clinical signs of chronic liver disease and decompensation
sessions: Case presentation:ALD, Hepatitis C with decompensation
los.html:
Signs of chronic liver diseaseSigns of decompensation
Hands: clubbing, leuconychia (low albumin), palmar erythema, Dupuytren's (alcohol)Jaundice
Spider naevi (>5, SVC territory), gynaecomastia, loss of body hair, testicular atrophy (oestrogen excess)Ascites (shifting dullness)
Bruising (low clotting factors), parotid enlargement (alcohol)Hepatic encephalopathy: confusion, drowsiness, asterixis, fetor hepaticus
Hepatomegaly (early) or small shrunken liverVariceal bleeding: haematemesis, melaena
Splenomegaly, caput medusae (portal hypertension)Coagulopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Muscle wasting, xanthelasma and scratch marks (PBC)
Precipitants of decompensationInfection (including SBP), GI bleeding, alcohol binge, constipation, drugs (sedatives, opioids, diuretics), dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, hypoglycaemia, HCC, portal vein thrombosis.
Severity scoresChild–Pugh (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy), MELD/UKELD (transplant listing).

los.text: Describe the effect of external agents on the liver (alcohol, viruses) and link them to clinical diseases.
los.html:
AgentMechanismClinical disease
Alcohol
  • Alcohol dehydrogenase → acetaldehyde (toxic, forms protein adducts) → acetate
  • Excess NADH drives fat synthesis
  • CYP2E1 induction → free radicals
  • Gut endotoxin activates Kupffer cells
  • Stellate cells lay down collagen
Fatty liver (reversible), alcoholic hepatitis (jaundice, fever, tender hepatomegaly, AST:ALT >2, high WCC; severe if Maddrey ≥32 → consider prednisolone), cirrhosis, HCC
Hepatitis AFaecal–oral; acuteAcute hepatitis, never chronic; vaccine
Hepatitis B (DNA)Blood, sexual, vertical; immune-mediated hepatocyte damage
  • Acute
  • Chronic in ~5% of adults but ~90% of neonates
  • Cirrhosis, HCC.
  • Serology: HBsAg (infection), anti-HBc IgM (acute), HBeAg (high infectivity), anti-HBs (immunity/vaccination), HBV DNA.
  • Treat chronic with tenofovir or entecavir
  • Vaccine
Hepatitis C (RNA)Blood (injecting drug use, transfusions before 1991, tattoos); low sexual and vertical risk~75% become chronic → cirrhosis, HCC; anti-HCV then HCV RNA PCR; direct-acting antivirals (8–12 weeks) cure >95%; no vaccine
Hepatitis DNeeds HBVWorse HBV disease
Hepatitis EUndercooked pork (UK genotype 3), faecal–oralUsually mild; chronic in the immunosuppressed; severe in pregnancy (genotype 1)
Paracetamol overdoseNAPQI accumulates when glutathione runs out → zone 3 necrosisAcute liver failure: acetylcysteine
Other drugsIdiosyncraticCo-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin (cholestasis), anti-TB drugs, methotrexate (fibrosis), amiodarone, valproate, nitrofurantoin, statins

los.text: Identify the complex health needs of homeless people and how to respond to these needs
los.html:
• Scale of harm: people experiencing homelessness die decades early (average age at death in the mid-40s)
    • tri-morbidity (physical illness + mental illness + substance misuse) is common.
Complex health needs
Infections: TB, hepatitis B and C, HIV, skin and wound infections, foot problems
Respiratory disease (COPD, asthma), dental disease, malnutrition
Alcohol and drug dependence, liver disease, overdose, seizures (alcohol withdrawal)
Mental illness, personality disorder, trauma, self-harm, acquired brain injury, cognitive impairment
Injuries and assaults; untreated chronic disease; frailty at a young age
  • Barriers: belief that an address or ID is needed to register with a GP (it isn't)
  • Rigid appointment systems
  • No phone or money
  • Stigma
  • Distrust
  • Survival needs come first
  • Frequent moves
  • How to respond:
    • Inclusion health services: outreach, specialist homeless GP practices, drop-ins, flexible appointments.
    • Trauma-informed, non-judgemental care; opportunistic care each contact (BBV testing, vaccinations, TB screening, foot and dental care).
    • Harm reduction: needle exchange, naloxone, opioid substitution.
    • Hospital: homeless (Pathway) teams, planned discharge (never discharge to the street), duty to refer to the local housing authority (Homelessness Reduction Act 2017 in England; Housing (Wales) Act 2014).
    • Housing First, MDT working, safeguarding.

los.text: Identify the liver and spleen, their anatomical relationships and link them to function and common pathology.
los.html:
LiverDetail
PositionRight upper quadrant under the diaphragm, protected by ribs 7–11; descends on inspiration (palpate from the RIF)
LobesRight, left, caudate, quadrate (8 functional Couinaud segments: basis of resection)
Blood supplyDual: portal vein (~75%, nutrient-rich) + hepatic artery (~25%, oxygenated) → sinusoids → hepatic veins → IVC
Porta hepatisPortal vein, hepatic artery, common hepatic duct
Relations
  • Gallbladder (inferior surface; fundus at the 9th costal cartilage: Murphy's sign)
  • Stomach
  • Duodenum
  • Right kidney (hepatorenal pouch of Morison: fluid collects here when supine)
  • Hepatic flexure
  • IVC
Clinical link
  • Portal hypertension opens portosystemic anastomoses: oesophageal varices (left gastric ↔ azygos), caput medusae (paraumbilical ↔ epigastric), rectal varices
  • and causes splenomegaly and ascites
SpleenDetail
Position
  • Left upper quadrant, under ribs 9–11 posteriorly
  • "1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11" (1 × 3 × 5 inches, 7 oz, ribs 9–11)
VesselsSplenic artery (coeliac trunk); splenic vein joins the SMV to form the portal vein
RelationsStomach, left kidney, splenic flexure, tail of pancreas, diaphragm
FunctionFilters old red cells, immune response to encapsulated bacteria, extramedullary haematopoiesis
Clinical link
  • Enlarges towards the RIF, has a notch, you can't get above it, dull to percussion
  • Causes: portal hypertension, haematological (CML, myelofibrosis: massive; lymphoma, haemolysis), infection (EBV, malaria), infiltration.
  • Rupture (trauma, EBV: avoid contact sport) → left shoulder tip pain (Kehr's sign).
  • After splenectomy: pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal and flu vaccines, antibiotic prophylaxis (risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection)

los.text: Explain the pharmacology of abused drugs to their clinically important effects.
los.html:
• Common pathway: drugs of abuse increase dopamine in the mesolimbic reward pathway (ventral tegmental area → nucleus accumbens), driving reinforcement and dependence.
DrugMechanismClinically important effects
AlcoholEnhances GABA-A, inhibits NMDA
  • Intoxication, accidents
  • Withdrawal (CNS hyperexcitability: tremor at 6–12 h, seizures at 12–48 h, delirium tremens at 48–72 h) → chlordiazepoxide + thiamine (Wernicke's)
  • Liver disease, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy
Opioids (heroin)μ-receptor agonists
  • Euphoria, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression → naloxone
  • Withdrawal (yawning, rhinorrhoea, dilated pupils, piloerection, diarrhoea, cramps: unpleasant, rarely dangerous)
  • Opioid substitution (methadone: full agonist, QT; buprenorphine: partial agonist)
  • Injecting → BBVs, abscesses, right-sided endocarditis, DVT
CocaineBlocks reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin; Na⁺ channel block
  • Sympathomimetic: tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, dilated pupils, chest pain (coronary vasospasm), MI, stroke, arrhythmias, agitation, psychosis
  • Treat with benzodiazepines (avoid beta-blockers)
  • with alcohol forms cocaethylene
Amphetamines, MDMARelease monoamines (MDMA mainly serotonin)Sympathomimetic; MDMA: hyperthermia, hyponatraemia (SIADH + drinking water), serotonin syndrome, rhabdomyolysis
BenzodiazepinesPositive modulators of GABA-ASedation, respiratory depression (especially with opioids/alcohol), dependence, withdrawal seizures
CannabisCB1 partial agonist (THC)Anxiety, psychosis (high potency, early use), cannabinoid hyperemesis (relieved by hot showers)
Synthetic cannabinoids ("spice")Full CB1 agonistsSevere agitation, seizures, psychosis, AKI
KetamineNMDA antagonistDissociation; ketamine bladder (ulcerative cystitis)
GHB/GBLGABA-B agonistSudden coma, respiratory depression, severe withdrawal
Nitrous oxideInactivates B12Subacute combined degeneration
NicotineNicotinic agonist → dopamine releaseDependence; harm is from tobacco smoke

los.text: Explain how alcohol and viral hepatitis C are major causes of chronic liver disease in this country; and to link the patient’s lifestyle as an aetiological factor; to be able to recognise clinical signs of chronic liver disease and decompensation
los.html:
• Integrated summary (see LOs 1–4 and 3 for detail):
QuestionAnswer
Why alcohol?Widely available and cheap; consumption above 14 units/week is common; dependence; drives fatty liver → hepatitis → cirrhosis
Why hepatitis C?
  • Injecting drug use
  • Silent for decades
  • Leads to cirrhosis and HCC
  • Now curable, so finding people (testing in drug services, prisons, A&E) matters
Lifestyle as causeAlcohol, injecting, obesity, diet and inactivity are modifiable: address them at every contact
Recognising chronic diseaseClubbing, leuconychia, palmar erythema, spider naevi, gynaecomastia, hepatosplenomegaly
Recognising decompensationJaundice, ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding (look for the precipitant: infection, bleeding, alcohol, constipation, drugs)
InvestigationsLFTs, albumin, INR, platelets (low: hypersplenism), hepatitis serology, ultrasound, FibroScan (elastography) or ELF/FIB-4 scores for fibrosis, ascitic tap (SBP: neutrophils >250/mm³).
Management
  • Alcohol abstinence (support, relapse-prevention drugs)
  • DAAs for hepatitis C
  • Weight loss for MASLD
  • Nutrition
  • 6-monthly ultrasound (± AFP) for HCC surveillance in cirrhosis
  • Endoscopy for varices (non-selective beta-blocker: carvedilol, or banding)
  • Ascites (salt restriction, spironolactone, paracentesis with albumin)
  • Encephalopathy (lactulose, rifaximin)
  • Transplant assessment.

los.text: Describe the functions of the liver including drug and alcohol metabolism.
los.html:
FunctionExamplesWhen it fails
SynthesisAlbumin, clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X are vitamin K-dependent), fibrinogen, transport proteins, CRPLow albumin (oedema, ascites, leuconychia), raised INR
Carbohydrate metabolismGlycogen storage, glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesisHypoglycaemia (acute liver failure)
Fat metabolismLipoproteins, cholesterol, β-oxidation, ketogenesisSteatosis
Protein metabolismDeamination, urea cycle (ammonia → urea)Raised ammonia → encephalopathy; low urea
BileBile salts for fat digestion and absorption of vitamins A, D, E, KSteatorrhoea, vitamin K deficiency
BilirubinUptake, conjugation (UGT1A1), excretion in bileJaundice
StorageGlycogen, vitamins A, D, B12, iron, copper
ImmuneKupffer cells clear gut bacteria and endotoxinInfections (SBP)
HormonesAngiotensinogen, IGF-1, thrombopoietin, hepcidin; breaks down oestrogen and aldosteroneLow platelets, spider naevi and gynaecomastia (oestrogen), secondary hyperaldosteronism (ascites)
Drug metabolism
  • Phase I: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis by cytochrome P450 (CYP3A4, 2D6, 2C9, 2E1); inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort, chronic alcohol) and inhibitors (clarithromycin, fluconazole, grapefruit, acute alcohol) cause interactions.
  • Phase II: conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation (slow acetylators: isoniazid), glutathione) → water-soluble products excreted in urine or bile.
  • First-pass metabolism: oral drugs pass through the liver first (GTN given sublingually to avoid it).
  • Paracetamol: mostly glucuronidated/sulfated; a little → NAPQI via CYP2E1, neutralised by glutathione; in overdose (or with induced CYP2E1, low glutathione from malnutrition) NAPQI damages hepatocytes → acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione.
Alcohol metabolism
  • Alcohol dehydrogenase (→ acetaldehyde) then aldehyde dehydrogenase (→ acetate), about 1 unit per hour
  • Chronic drinking induces CYP2E1 (MEOS) → tolerance
  • Disulfiram blocks ALDH (acetaldehyde build-up: flushing, nausea)
  • ALDH2 deficiency causes flushing in some East Asian people.
Prescribing in liver disease
  • Reduced clearance (opioids, benzodiazepines can precipitate encephalopathy)
  • Low albumin raises free drug levels
  • Coagulopathy (warfarin sensitivity)
  • Avoid NSAIDs (renal failure, bleeding)
  • Avoid hepatotoxins
  • Use the BNF hepatic impairment advice.

los.text: Elicit a structured and relevant history from a patient presenting with jaundice, focusing on risk factors, timeline, and systemic symptoms
los.html:
TypeClues in historyBilirubin
Pre-hepatic (haemolysis, Gilbert's)Anaemia symptoms, normal stools and urine colour; Gilbert's: mild jaundice with fasting or illnessUnconjugated
HepaticViral prodrome (fever, malaise, anorexia), alcohol, drugs (paracetamol, co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin, herbal remedies), travel (hepatitis A/E), injecting, sexual history, tattoos, transfusions, autoimmune diseaseMixed
Post-hepatic (obstructive)
  • Pale stools, dark urine, itching
  • RUQ colic (gallstones)
  • Fever and rigors + RUQ pain + jaundice (Charcot's triad: cholangitis)
  • Painless jaundice with weight loss (pancreatic head cancer: Courvoisier's law: palpable, painless gallbladder)
  • IBD (PSC)
Conjugated
  • Structure: onset (sudden or gradual), duration and progression
    • systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, anorexia, abdominal swelling, confusion, GI bleeding, itch)
    • risk factors above
    • alcohol (units, pattern, dependence: AUDIT)
    • PMH (gallstones, IBD, autoimmune), family history (haemochromatosis, Wilson's, Gilbert's), vaccinations
    • ICE.

los.text: Demonstrate a gastrointestinal examination, recognising and interpreting signs suggestive of liver disease
los.html:
SignInterpretation
Jaundice (sclera), scratch marksHyperbilirubinaemia; cholestasis
Clubbing, leuconychia, palmar erythema, spider naevi, gynaecomastia, loss of body hair, Dupuytren'sChronic liver disease (alcohol for Dupuytren's)
Asterixis, confusion, fetor hepaticusHepatic encephalopathy
Hepatomegaly: smooth (fatty liver, hepatitis, heart failure; pulsatile in tricuspid regurgitation), craggy (metastases, HCC)
Splenomegaly, caput medusae, ascites (shifting dullness)Portal hypertension
Palpable painless gallbladder in a jaundiced patientCourvoisier's sign: likely pancreatic or distal bile duct cancer (not stones)
Tender RUQ with inspiratory catchMurphy's sign: cholecystitis
Kayser–Fleischer ringsWilson's disease
Bronze skinHaemochromatosis
Bruising, muscle wasting, parotid swellingCoagulopathy, malnutrition, alcohol
  • Present: "Signs of chronic liver disease (palmar erythema, spider naevi, gynaecomastia), with evidence of portal hypertension (splenomegaly, ascites) and decompensation (jaundice, asterixis), suggesting decompensated cirrhosis, likely alcohol-related."

los.text: Explain a clinical diagnosis clearly and compassionately, using language that any patient can understand
los.html:
• Example: explaining alcohol-related cirrhosis:
StepExample wording
Find out what they know"What have you been told about your liver so far?"
Warning shot"The scan results are more serious than we'd hoped."
Plain language, small chunks
  • "Your liver has become scarred.
  • This happens when it's been damaged over many years, and alcohol is the main reason in your case."
Pause, empathySilence; "This is a lot to take in."
What it means"The liver can't do all its jobs as well, so fluid can build up and it's harder to fight infection."
Hope and action
  • "Stopping alcohol completely is the most important thing: it can stop the damage getting worse and the liver can recover some function.
  • We'll support you with that."
PlanAlcohol support, diet, 6-monthly scans, a camera test to look for swollen veins
Safety-netSeek help urgently for yellow eyes, tummy swelling, confusion, vomiting blood or black stools
Check understandingTeach-back; written information (e.g. British Liver Trust)
  • Avoid jargon ("cirrhosis" without explanation, "decompensation", "varices"), blame, and information overload.

los.text: Apply motivational interviewing techniques to support and encourage a patient in making behaviour changes relevant to their health (e.g., alcohol reduction)
los.html:
• Spirit of MI: partnership
    • acceptance
    • compassion and evocation (drawing out the patient's own reasons to change)
    • rather than telling them what to do.
Skill (OARS)Example
Open questions"How does drinking fit into your life at the moment?"
Affirmations"You've done really well to cut down already."
Reflective listening"Part of you enjoys drinking, but part of you is worried about your liver."
SummariesPull together their reasons for change
Principles
  • Express empathy
  • Develop discrepancy (between current behaviour and their goals)
  • Roll with resistance (avoid the "righting reflex": arguing makes people defend the status quo)
  • Support self-efficacy.
Elicit change talk
  • Desire, Ability, Reasons, Need → Commitment, Activation, Taking steps
  • Importance and confidence rulers ("On a scale of 0–10, how important is cutting down? Why a 6 and not a 3?").
Stages of change(Prochaska and DiClemente)Pre-contemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance (± relapse): match the approach to the stage.
Alcohol specifics
  • AUDIT-C screening, brief intervention (FRAMES), refer to alcohol services
  • Dependent drinkers mustn't stop suddenly (withdrawal seizures): medically assisted withdrawal (chlordiazepoxide, thiamine)
  • Relapse prevention: acamprosate, naltrexone, disulfiram.

los.text: Apply respectful, inclusive, and person-centred communication when interacting with transgender patients
los.html:
PracticeDetail
Introduce yourself with your pronounsInvites the patient to share theirs
Ask, don't assume"What name would you like me to use?" "What pronouns do you use?"
Use them consistently; if you get it wrong, apologise briefly and move on
RecordsMake sure the correct name and gender are recorded (patients can change these on NHS records)
Inclusive languageAsk about anatomy relevant to the problem rather than assuming; e.g. "people with a cervix" for screening
Focus on the presenting problemDon't ask about transition unless relevant
Privacy and confidentialityGender history is sensitive; disclosing someone's gender recognition information without consent can be an offence (Gender Recognition Act 2004)
RespectSame dignity as any patient; offer a chaperone; gender reassignment is a protected characteristic (Equality Act 2010)

los.text: Recognise appropriate contexts to ask sensitively about gender transition history, ensuring relevance and respect for privacy
los.html:
Relevant contextWhy
MedicationsOestrogen (VTE risk, interactions), testosterone (polycythaemia, acne, lipids), anti-androgens, puberty blockers
Anatomy and surgery
  • Organ-based screening and differentials: cervical screening for trans men with a cervix
  • Breast screening
  • The prostate remains after vaginoplasty
  • Pregnancy possible if uterus and ovaries present
InvestigationsReference ranges (Hb, creatinine) depend on hormone status
Fertility and sexual healthContraception, STI risk, fertility preservation
Mental healthContext of stress and discrimination
  • How: explain why you're asking ("Because it affects which tests you need, can I ask about any surgery or hormones?")
    • ask about current anatomy and medications rather than the whole history
    • never ask out of curiosity
    • document only what's clinically needed.

los.text: Identify and describe barriers transgender individuals face in accessing healthcare, and outline challenges healthcare providers may encounter in delivering inclusive care
los.html:
Barriers for trans peopleChallenges for providers
Discrimination and previous negative experiences → avoiding or delaying careLimited training and knowledge
Misgendering, deadnaming, intrusive questionsEvolving, debated evidence (e.g. the Cass Review 2024 on young people's gender services)
Very long waits for gender identity clinicsUncertainty about shared-care prescribing of hormones
Screening invitations based on recorded gender (missed cervical/breast screening)IT systems that don't handle gender changes well
Fear of being outed; mental health stigmaTime pressure, fear of "getting it wrong"
Costs of private care; social and economic disadvantage; intersecting disadvantage (ethnicity, disability)Balancing confidentiality with clinical need
  • Improving care: training
    • inclusive policies and forms
    • clear guidance (GMC, NHS)
    • partnership with specialist services
    • manual screening recall where needed
    • a respectful culture.

los.text: Identify the lobes and ligaments of the liver, their anatomical relations, the peritoneal reflections and movements during respiration
los.html:
Position
  • Right upper quadrant under the diaphragm, mostly behind the ribs (5th intercostal space to the costal margin)
  • Moves down with inspiration (palpate the edge as the patient breathes in).
Anatomical lobes
  • Right (largest) and left, divided by the falciform ligament in front
  • The caudate (behind, next to the IVC) and quadrate (below, next to the gallbladder) lobes belong functionally to the left.
Ligament / reflectionDetail
Falciform ligamentAnterior abdominal wall → liver; free edge carries the ligamentum teres (umbilical vein remnant)
Coronary ligaments (anterior and posterior layers)Reflect from the diaphragm, enclosing the bare area (no peritoneum)
Left and right triangular ligamentsEnds of the coronary ligament
Lesser omentumHepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments (free edge holds the portal triad)
Ligamentum venosumDuctus venosus remnant, in a fissure on the visceral surface
RelationStructures
Diaphragmatic surfaceDiaphragm, (pleura and lungs above it), anterior abdominal wall
Visceral surfaceStomach, duodenum, gallbladder, right colic flexure, right kidney and suprarenal (hepatorenal pouch: Morison's pouch)
BehindIVC (in a groove on the bare area), oesophagus

los.text: Identify at the porta hepatis (the hilum of the liver): the hepatic artery, the hepatic portal vein, and the hepatic ducts.
los.html:
• Porta hepatis: transverse fissure on the visceral surface between the caudate (behind) and quadrate (in front) lobes.
StructurePosition (front → back)
Common hepatic duct (right and left hepatic ducts)Front
Hepatic artery proper (right and left branches)Middle
Hepatic portal vein (right and left branches)Back
Also
  • Hepatic nerve plexus and lymph nodes.
  • The hepatic veins do not leave here: they drain straight into the IVC on the back of the liver.
Pringle manoeuvreClamp the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of the lesser omentum) to stop inflow during liver bleeding.

los.text: Summarise the functional anatomy of the portal vein, the portal venous system and portalsystemic anastomoses and their significance in portal hypertension.
los.html:
Portal vein
  • Formed behind the neck of the pancreas (L1) by the superior mesenteric vein + splenic vein (IMV usually joins the splenic)
  • → up behind the 1st part of duodenum
  • → in the free edge of the lesser omentum
  • → porta hepatis.
  • Carries ~75% of liver blood flow (nutrients, toxins, drugs: first-pass metabolism).
Portal hypertension(usually cirrhosis)Blood diverts through portosystemic anastomoses:
SitePortal sideSystemic sideResult
Lower oesophagusLeft gastric veinOesophageal veins → azygosOesophageal varices (life-threatening bleeding)
Anorectal junctionSuperior rectal veinMiddle and inferior rectal veinsRectal varices
UmbilicusParaumbilical veins (along ligamentum teres)Superficial epigastric veinsCaput medusae
RetroperitoneumColic veinsLumbar, renal veinsRetroperitoneal varices
Bare area of liverLiver veinsPhrenic veins
  • Other effects: splenomegaly (hypersplenism → low platelets), ascites. TIPS (shunt from portal to hepatic vein) reduces the pressure.

los.text: Identify the position (in relation to the ribs) and form of the spleen in relation to its palpation through the abdominal wall and its key anatomical relationships with other abdominal structures.
los.html:
Position
  • Left hypochondrium, under ribs 9–11, its long axis along the 10th rib
  • Does not usually reach in front of the midaxillary line
  • ~12 × 7 × 3 cm ("1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11": 1 × 3 × 5 inches, 7 oz, ribs 9–11).
FormDiaphragmatic (convex) and visceral surfaces; notched superior border (felt when enlarged); hilum.
Palpation
  • Normal spleen is not palpable
  • It must enlarge about 3 times to be felt.
  • It enlarges down and towards the right iliac fossa
  • You can't get above it
  • It has a notch
  • Moves with breathing
  • and is dull to percussion (unlike a kidney, which is ballotable and has a band of resonance over it).
RelationStructure
BehindDiaphragm, ribs 9–11 (and pleura and lung base above)
Front (visceral surface)Stomach
BelowSplenic (left colic) flexure
MediallyLeft kidney, tail of pancreas

los.text: Explain the significance of the anatomical relationships of the spleen in relation to trauma, chronic infections and disorders of the haematopoietic system.
los.html:
SituationWhy the anatomy matters
Trauma
  • Thin capsule
  • Very vascular
  • Under ribs 9–11: fractured left lower ribs can lacerate it → haemorrhage
  • Shock
  • Left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign) from blood irritating the diaphragm
Enlargement (chronic infection: malaria, EBV, endocarditis; haematological: CML, myelofibrosis, lymphoma, haemolytic anaemias; portal hypertension)
  • Enlarged spleen leaves the protection of the ribs → easier to rupture (contact sports avoided in glandular fever)
  • Hypersplenism traps cells
Splenectomy
  • Risk to the tail of pancreas (in the splenorenal ligament) → pancreatic fistula
  • and to the stomach (short gastric vessels)
  • Afterwards lifelong risk of encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib): vaccinate and give antibiotics
HaematopoiesisThe spleen makes blood cells in the fetus and can do so again in marrow failure (extramedullary haematopoiesis)
  • Accessory spleens (splenunculi, ~10%): near the hilum; can cause relapse after splenectomy for ITP.

los.text: Identify the splenic artery and vein.
los.html:
Splenic artery
  • Largest branch of the coeliac trunk
  • → runs to the left, tortuous, along the upper border of the pancreas
  • → through the splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament
  • → splits into ~5 branches at the hilum (segmental end arteries → splenic infarcts).
Branches on the wayPancreatic branches, short gastric arteries (fundus) and left gastroepiploic artery (greater curvature), via the gastrosplenic ligament.
Splenic veinFrom the hilum runs behind the pancreas (below the artery), receives the inferior mesenteric vein, joins the SMV behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein.
Clinical
  • Splenic artery aneurysm (rupture in pregnancy)
  • Splenic vein thrombosis (pancreatitis) → gastric varices
  • Posterior duodenal ulcers can erode the gastroduodenal artery (not splenic).

los.text: Identify the peritoneum surrounding the spleen and the two ligaments it forms (lienorenal and gastrosplenic).
los.html:
• Peritoneum: the spleen is intraperitoneal, covered by peritoneum except at the hilum; it lies in the dorsal mesogastrium.
LigamentJoinsContains
Gastrosplenic ligamentGreater curvature of stomach → hilumShort gastric vessels, left gastroepiploic vessels
Lienorenal (splenorenal) ligamentLeft kidney → hilumSplenic artery and vein, tail of pancreas
  • Both form the boundaries of the lesser sac on the left.
  • Clinical: dividing the splenorenal ligament mobilises the spleen at splenectomy; the phrenicocolic ligament supports its lower pole.

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the attachments, openings and relationships of the diaphragm, the surface anatomy and the movements it makes during breathing.
los.html:
• Attachments: sternal part (xiphoid), costal part (lower 6 costal cartilages and ribs), lumbar part (right crus L1–3, left crus L1–2; medial and lateral arcuate ligaments over psoas and quadratus lumborum; median arcuate ligament over the aorta) → all insert into the central tendon.
OpeningLevelTransmits
CavalT8 (central tendon)IVC, right phrenic nerve branches
OesophagealT10 (right crus muscle)Oesophagus, vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of left gastric vessels
AorticT12 (behind the median arcuate ligament)Aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein
"I 8 10 Eggs At 12"IVC 8, (o)Esophagus 10, Aorta 12.
Surface anatomy
  • Domes reach the 5th rib (right) and 5th intercostal space (left) in expiration
  • The central tendon at the xiphisternal joint (T9).
Breathing
  • Contraction flattens the domes (descends ~1.5 cm in quiet breathing, up to ~10 cm in deep) → chest volume increases, abdominal pressure rises
  • The crura also act as a sphincter at the oesophageal opening (reflux, hiatus hernia).
RelationsAbove: pleura, lungs, heart (pericardium fused to the central tendon); below: liver, stomach, spleen, kidneys and suprarenals.

los.text: Identify the structures that pass through the diaphragm.
los.html:
StructureThrough
IVCCaval opening (T8)
Right phrenic nerveCaval opening
Oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of left gastric artery and veinOesophageal hiatus (T10)
Aorta, thoracic duct, azygos (and hemiazygos) veinAortic hiatus (T12, behind the diaphragm)
Left phrenic nervePierces the left dome
Greater, lesser and least splanchnic nervesPierce the crura
Sympathetic trunksBehind the medial arcuate ligaments
Superior epigastric vesselsSternocostal triangle (foramen of Morgagni)
Subcostal nerve and vesselsBehind the lateral arcuate ligament
  • Hernias: hiatus hernia (sliding or rolling, at the oesophageal hiatus); congenital Bochdalek (posterolateral, left) and Morgagni (anterior) hernias.

los.text: Identify and describe the locations of the 8 segments of the liver.
los.html:
• Couinaud segments: 8 functional segments, each with its own portal vein branch, hepatic artery branch and bile duct in the centre, and hepatic veins between them.
    • Each can be resected on its own.
SegmentLocation
ICaudate lobe (drains straight into the IVC; spared in Budd–Chiari)
II, IIILeft lateral (II above, III below)
IV (IVa above, IVb below)Left medial (includes the quadrate lobe)
V, VIIIRight anterior (V below, VIII above)
VI, VIIRight posterior (VI below, VII above)
NumberingClockwise from segment I, as if looking at the front of the liver (II–VIII round the clock).
Dividing planes
  • The middle hepatic vein (Cantlie's line: gallbladder fossa to IVC) separates the functional right and left livers
  • The right and left hepatic veins divide the sectors
  • The portal vein branches divide upper from lower.
ClinicalSurgeons remove segments or hemi-livers (hepatectomy) for tumours or live donation; imaging reports lesions by segment.
